newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco industry charges FDA seeks to shut it down.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco industry charges FDA seeks to shut it down.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
The Food and Drug Administration is seeking powers that ultimately could be used to shut down the tobacco industry in the United States, a lawyer for cigarette companies told a federal court Monday.

"The FDA is asserting power to ban this industry," Richard Cooper, an attorney representing cigarette makers, said as U.S. District Judge William Osteen Sr. opened a one-day hearing in the tobacco industry's lawsuit against the FDA.

"It's not going to exercise that power for now ... but it has expressly reserved this momentous power for the future," Cooper said as tobacco companies pressed their claim that the FDA was trying to control cigarettes unlawfully.

Cooper, a former chief counsel for the FDA who is now with the Washington firm of Williams & Connolly, said the federal agency's proposed new regulations of tobacco were "an extraordinary assertion of power."

After the hearing, FDA Commissioner David Kessler told reporters that President Clinton "stands firmly behind the regulations to try in a common-sense way to reduce the number of children who will become addicted.
"We think the case is a strong one," said Kessler. "What is at stake is the future health of so many of our children."
The judge is expected to be the first to rule on whether the FDA has the right to regulate cigarette sales and marketing and whether the proposed rules are constitutional.

Monday's arguments focused on the tobacco industry's motion for summary judgment, in which the judge has been asked to make a decision on the merits of the case without a trial. If Osteen feels he needs additional evidence, he will schedule a trial in the near future.

The judge said he hoped to render a decision within five to 10 weeks. The first set of FDA rules is set to take effect Feb. 28 and will require retailers to ask for photo identification of youthful purchasers.

Regardless of the outcome of Monday's hearing, it is expected that Osteen's ruling will be appealed to the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals based in Richmond, Va., and most likely to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Monday's battle dates back to August 1995, when Clinton authorized the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children.

The FDA rules would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales, ban sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.
The rules would restrict advertising in some publications and require retailers to see photo identification for cigarette purchasers under 27 years old.

Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina, all major tobacco-growing states, have filed court papers urging the court to overturn the regulations. But at least 33 states, along with San Francisco and Guam, are supporting the rules.

The tobacco industry and other plaintiffs argued three challenges during the hearing. In the first two arguments, they alleged Congress never intended for the FDA to regulate tobacco products and that tobacco is not a medical device or drug as defined by the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act.

In the third set of arguments, they alleged the advertising restrictions violate the First Amendment because they are too broad and that there are other ways the FDA could reduce underage smoking without limiting commercial advertising directed at adults.
Osteen could use any of the three arguments to invalidate all of the rules.

Cooper argued that Congress has "carved in stone" its intention that the FDA should be excluded from regulating tobacco. He said Congress has enacted its own comprehensive tobacco program, including health warnings on cigarettes, rather than giving the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products.
He said it specifically rejected two bills that would have given the FDA jurisdiction over cigarettes and smokeless tobacco.
"If new interpretation of the law is needed here ... then that problem should be taken to Congress," Cooper said.
He also said that the FDA in 1965 told Congress it had no such jurisdiction and had not sought such control until last year.

George Phillips, a Justice Department lawyer representing the FDA, argued that the administration had not been prohibited from regulating cigarettes and that the Supreme Court has held that federal regulatory agencies are responsible for continuing evaluations of new evidence and developments in appropriate areas.

He said the FDA has an extremely reasonable basis for changing its position on tobacco products because of new evidence about nicotine addiction and the industry's knowledge about how nicotine affects smokers that has surfaced in the last 10 years.
Phillips alleged the new evidence shows tobacco companies "control the level of nicotine in cigarettes" and that the industry "knew clearly of the addictive qualities of cigarettes."
Tobacco companies maintain they do not "spike" cigarettes with nicotine and that nicotine is not addictive.
